extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of Schopenhauer's epistemology: how perception, understanding, causality, subject/object relations, dreams, and animal cognition should be construed. Focuses on criteria that distinguish sensation, perception, truth, illusion, and kinds of cognitive defect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception as intellectual (not mere sensation)
rubrics_metrics.description: “perception is not merely of the senses, but intellectual—that is, pure knowledge through the understanding of the cause from the effect.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perception is the immediate, necessary and certain method of knowing of the pure understanding; without it there would be only a dull plant-like consciousness of changes. Sensory data are merely the material; the understanding converts these data into perception by passing from effect to cause. Examples/explanations cited: single vision from two eyes, double vision in squint, upright appearance though retinal image inverted, stereoscope; cited reference to essay on 'Light and Colour' and 'Principle of Sufficient Reason'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law of causality is a priori for perception
rubrics_metrics.description: “the knowledge of causality is included in perception in general... and therefore in respect of experience is completely a priori, does not presuppose it, but is presupposed by it as a condition.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle is offered as a refutation of Hume’s doctrine that causality results from experience: because perception presupposes causality, causality cannot be derived from experience. The passage argues that all experience depends upon this a priori principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not treat subject–object relation as cause–effect
rubrics_metrics.description: “It is needful to guard against the grave error of supposing that because perception arises through the knowledge of causality, the relation of subject and object is that of cause and effect.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The causal relation subsists only between immediate object and objects known indirectly (i.e., between objects), not between subject and object. Confusing these leads to the realism/idealism controversy and to scepticism. The principle of sufficient reason applies to objects (their form, being), not to the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical (awakening) criterion to distinguish dream from waking
rubrics_metrics.description: “The only sure criterion by which to distinguish them is in fact the entirely empirical one of awaking, through which at any rate the causal connection between dreamed events and those of waking life, is distinctly and sensibly broken off.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kant’s causal-continuity test is discussed but criticised as practically inadequate because we cannot trace causal links; thus awakening (the observable break of causal continuity) is the reliable empirical test. Hobbes's remark (sleeping in clothes causing confusions) is cited as supporting evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kant’s causal-continuity criterion for dream vs reality (criticised)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Kant answers the question thus: 'The connection of ideas among themselves, according to the law of causality, constitutes the difference between real life and dreams.'”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Schopenhauer notes that this criterion fails in practice because individual dreams can have internal causal coherence; thus while theoretically plausible (long dream/life vs short dreams), it is not a practical rule except in special cases where causal continuity can be checked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perception is constructed by comparing impressions of various senses
rubrics_metrics.description: “the understanding constructs perceptions out of the data supplied by the senses; how by comparison of the impressions which the various senses receive from the object, a child arrives at perceptions.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as the mechanism by which the single perception emerges from distinct sensory inputs; it explains phenomena such as single vision from two eyes, double vision, stereoscopic effects and illusions arising from sudden alteration of sense-organs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Body as immediate object vs body as object proper
rubrics_metrics.description: “the body is for us immediate object; that is to say, that idea which forms the starting-point of the subject’s knowledge... the body as object proper, that is, as an idea perceived in space, is first known indirectly, like all other objects, through the application of the law of causality.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sensation supplies the body as immediate object (changes felt directly); the spatial, extended form of the body becomes known only via understanding applying causality (e.g. blind persons learn form via touch over time). A blind man without hands could never form his body's shape—illustrates dependence on causal inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between understanding and reason
rubrics_metrics.description: “Understanding is the same in all animals... knowledge of causality, transition from effect to cause... Reason... can only serve to take up the objective connections which are immediately known by the understanding, to make them permanent for thought.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding gives immediate apprehension of causal relations (perception/reality); reason deals in abstract concepts and truths (distinct, discursive). Reason makes immediate insights communicable and allows abstract judgments; understanding is non-reflective and immediate. Examples: scientific discoveries as flashes of understanding (Hooke, Newton, Lavoisier, Goethe).

rubrics_metrics.name: Error vs illusion: different faculties and remedies
rubrics_metrics.description: “That which is correctly known by reason is truth... that which is correctly known by understanding is reality... Error is opposed to truth... Illusion is opposed to reality.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Error = deception of reason (judgment on insufficient grounds) and can be corrected by abstract truths (reason). Illusion = deception of the understanding (immediate perception misattributes cause) and often persists despite abstract explanation; understanding assumes the commoner cause when two causes produce same effect. Examples of illusion: stick in water, reflections in spherical mirrors, moon-size at horizon.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of illusion (mechanism and examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Illusion takes place when the same effect may be attributed to two causes, of which one occurs very frequently, the other very seldom; the understanding... always assumes the presence of the commoner cause.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the understanding operates immediately and non-discursively, it picks the more common cause without deliberation, producing a perceptual illusion. Specific examples: broken appearance of stick in water, convex/concave mirror reflections, apparent greater extension of moon at horizon (attributed by understanding to distance via atmospheric perspective). Reason can state the true cause but cannot dispel the illusion itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mapping cognitive deficiencies to moral/psychological labels
rubrics_metrics.description: “Deficiency of understanding is called stupidity... deficiency in the application of reason to practice we shall recognise later as foolishness: deficiency of judgment as silliness, and lastly, partial or entire deficiency of memory as madness.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides diagnostic criteria: stupidity = dulness in applying law of causality (lack of keenness in inferring causes); illustrative anecdote: imbecile boy fascinated by reflections because he cannot infer causation. Distinguishes types of cognitive failure by faculty (understanding, reason, judgment, memory).

rubrics_metrics.name: Animals possess understanding a priori; distinction from instinct and reason
rubrics_metrics.description: “It follows... that all animals, even the least developed, have understanding... understanding is the same in all animals and in all men; it has everywhere the same simple form... For it is this that constitutes them animals... Whereas plants have only movement following on stimuli.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding (knowledge of causality) is present across animal species and is prior to experience; degree varies by species. Examples: elephant refusing unsafe bridge (inference of weight effect), orang‑outangs warming by fire but not maintaining it (shows lack of abstract deliberation/reason). Instinct is distinct from both understanding and reason. Criterion for animal vs plant: animals move from motives determined by knowledge; plants move from stimuli.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological principle: start from the idea (form) rather than subject or object
rubrics_metrics.description: “we did not start either from the object or the subject, but from the idea, which contains and presupposes them both; for the antithesis of object and subject is its primary, universal and essential form.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinguishes Schopenhauer’s method from other systems that try to explain one from the other via principle of sufficient reason. He confines the principle to objects and denies its validity for the subject–object relation; criticises philosophies (e.g., Fichte, philosophy of identity) that attempt to treat identity/intellectual intuition as escaping the alternatives.
